name: CT-RATE
description: CT-RATE is a public dataset that pairs 3D medical images with corresponding textual reports. It comprises 25,692 non-contrast 3D chest CT scans from 21,304 unique patients, totaling 50,188 reconstructed 3D chest CT volumes (over 14.3 million 2D slices). Each scan is accompanied by its corresponding radiology report including impression and findings sections. Each volume is also annotated with 18 abnormalities. The dataset is used to develop CT-CLIP (a CT-focused contrastive language-image pretraining framework) and CT-CHAT (a vision-language foundational chat model for 3D chest CT volumes).
creator: Ibrahim Ethem Hamamci, Sezgin Er, Chenyu Wang, Furkan Almas, Ayse Gulnihan Simsek, Sewal Nil Esirgun, Irem Dogan, Omer Faruk Durugol, Benjamin Hou, Suprosanna Shit, Weicheng Dai, Murong Xu, Hadrien Reynaud, Muhammed Furkan Dasdelen, Bastian Wittmann, Tamaz Amiranashvili, Enis Simsar, Mehmet Simsar, Emine Bensu Erdemir, Abdullah Alanbay, Anjany Sekuboyina, Berkan Lafci, Ahmet Kaplan, Zhiyong Lu, Malgorzata Polacin, Bernhard Kainz, Christian Bluethgen, Kayhan Batmanghelich, Mehmet Kemal Ozdemir, Bjoern Menze
publisher: University of Zurich / ETH Zurich / Istanbul Medipol University
citeAs: Hamamci, I.E., Er, S., Wang, C., et al. Generalist foundation models from a multimodal dataset for 3D computed tomography. arXiv:2403.17834v5 [cs.CV] (2026).
rai:dataCollection: CT-RATE was curated from Istanbul Medipol University Mega Hospital. It includes non-contrast chest CT volumes acquired between May 2015 and January 2023, totaling 50,188 reconstructed CT volumes from 25,692 distinct CT experiments conducted on 21,304 unique patients. CT volumes are reconstructed using various techniques to suit different window settings. Radiology reports were authored by radiologists and structured into four sections: clinical information, technique, findings, and impression. Reports were originally in Turkish and translated to English using the Google Translate API, with bilingual final-year medical students reviewing and correcting all translations. All patient and medical professional identifying information was anonymized from both reports and CT volume metadata.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Document analysis, Manual Human Curator
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The RAD-ChestCT dataset lacks a Mosaic attenuation label, which was excluded from external evaluation. The RAD-ChestCT dataset also lacks paired radiology reports, restricting report-to-volume retrieval evaluation to the internal validation set. Detailed metadata for the second external validation set (UPMC) is not publicly available as it is a private dataset.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Non-contrast chest CT volumes and corresponding radiology text reports from Istanbul Medipol University Mega Hospital, acquired between May 2015 and January 2023. CT volumes were acquired using Philips (61.5%), Siemens (30.1%), and PNMS (8.4%) CT scanners. Volumes are provided in resolutions of 512x512 px (65.4%), 768x768 px (4.2%), and 1024x1024 px (30.4%). Pixel spacing in the axial plane ranges from 0.227 to 1.416 mm, slice thickness from 0.035 to 6 mm, and number of slices per volume from 100 to 600.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Reports were anonymized by removing personal information using regular expressions to identify and eliminate date-related information and patient-doctor identifiers. Reports were translated from Turkish to English using the Google Translate API. CT volumes were anonymized by removing identifying information from metadata. Volumes involving contrast material or body parts other than the chest were excluded. CT volume orientation was standardized by examining metadata. Multi-abnormality labels were extracted from radiology reports using a finetuned text classifier (RadBERT-RoBERTa-4m). A visual question-answering (VQA) dataset of over 2.7 million question-answer pairs was derived from CT-RATE using Llama 3.1 7B/8B. Organ-level anatomical segmentation labels were generated using a state-of-the-art segmentation model (TotalSegmentator).
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Each CT volume was resized to achieve uniform spacing of 0.75 mm in the x-axis and y-axis and 1.5 mm in the z-axis. Volumes were then center-cropped or padded to a consistent resolution of 480x480x240. CT volumes were converted to Hounsfield Unit (HU) values using intercept and slope values from metadata. HU values were clipped to a range of -1000 to 1000. During training, values were normalized to a range of -1 to 1. For the CT-Net baseline, chest CT volumes were resized to 420x420x402. The same preprocessing pipeline was applied to external validation datasets.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Multi-abnormality labels for 18 distinct abnormalities were extracted from radiology reports using an automated text classifier. To develop this classifier, 1,000 reports were manually annotated by merging findings and impression sections, creating a multi-label dataset identifying 18 abnormalities. Conditions not referenced in either section were considered absent. Similar conditions were grouped (e.g., left and right mucoid impactions under mucoid impaction; various lung opacities under lung opacity; lung and fissural nodules as lung nodules). The annotated reports were divided into training (80%, 800 reports) and validation (20%, 200 reports) sets. The RadBERT-RoBERTa-4m model was finetuned on this dataset and applied to classify the remaining 24,692 reports. For CT-CHAT evaluation, three board-certified radiologists independently rated 150 reports for each model (CT-CHAT, RadFM, CT2Rep) on a 0-10 scale based on predefined clinical criteria covering finding description, localisation, terminology, and overall clinical adequacy.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The finetuned text encoder (RadBERT-RoBERTa-4m) achieved high precision, recall, and F1 scores across all 18 abnormalities (most above 0.95). For expert radiologist evaluation of report generation, cases were stratified by Llama score into low (0-3), medium (4-6), and high (7-10) clinical accuracy ranges, with 50 cases selected from each range to ensure balanced difficulty. Three radiologists scored reports independently; CT-CHAT achieved mean scores of 3.44 (R1), 4.10 (R2), and 4.52 (R3), outperforming RadFM and CT2Rep.
rai:annotationsPerItem: Each CT volume is annotated with 18 abnormality labels. For the expert radiologist evaluation, each of 150 selected reports was rated by 3 board-certified radiologists.
rai:annotatorDemographics: Manual annotation of 1,000 reports for the text classifier training was performed by the research team. Translation review was performed by bilingual final-year medical students. Expert radiologist evaluation was conducted by two board-certified thoracic radiologists from Zurich (R1, R2) and one from Istanbul (R3).
rai:machineAnnotationTools: RadBERT-RoBERTa-4m (finetuned for automated abnormality label extraction from radiology reports); Llama 3.1 8B (for generating VQA question-answer pairs); Llama 3.1 70B (for clinical accuracy evaluation/Llama score); TotalSegmentator (for organ-level anatomical segmentation labels); Google Translate API (for Turkish-to-English report translation); TotalSegmentator for pulmonary nodule segmentation (lobar location, centroid, diameters, volumes).
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: CT-RATE is publicly accessible via HuggingFace (https://huggingface.co/datasets/ibrahimhamamci/CT-RATE). The authors plan to extend CT-RATE with multi-abnormality segmentation and localization labels for 3D chest CT volumes as future work. Organ-level anatomical segmentation labels are openly available through the CT-RATE repository on Hugging Face. Trained models and codebase are publicly available at https://github.com/ibrahimethemhamamci/CT-CLIP and https://github.com/ibrahimethemhamamci/CT-CHAT.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Patient age (range 18-102 years, mean 48.8, mode 40), patient sex (41.6% female, 58.4% male). All personal information was anonymized: patient and medical professional identifiers were removed from reports and metadata before open-sourcing. CT volumes and metadata were de-identified.
rai:dataSocialImpact: CT-RATE addresses the scarcity of comprehensive 3D medical imaging datasets paired with textual reports, enabling development of AI foundation models for 3D medical imaging. The dataset and derived models (CT-CLIP, CT-CHAT) have the potential to reduce radiologist workload, improve diagnostic accuracy, and support patient care in settings where immediate radiological expertise is unavailable. The open-source release lays groundwork for future innovations in medical AI.
rai:dataBiases: CT-RATE is a single-institution dataset from Istanbul Medipol University Mega Hospital in Turkey, which may introduce biases related to a single geographic and clinical setting, potentially limiting generalizability to other populations. The dataset reflects real-world heterogeneity in CT scanners, acquisition protocols, and reconstruction techniques, but does not represent multiple institutions or diverse international populations. CT-CLIP depends on the specific terminology used in reports and the choice of prompts during zero-shot detection, and variability in disease description across radiology reports can affect detection accuracy.
rai:dataLimitations: CT-RATE is a single-center dataset, which may limit generalizability to other populations and clinical settings. Models are currently limited to chest CT volumes and do not cover other 3D imaging modalities (MRI, PET) or other anatomical regions. CT-CHAT's report generation quality remains insufficient for clinical deployment. The absence of true 3D VQA baselines limits benchmarking. The RAD-ChestCT external validation set lacks paired radiology reports. Multi-abnormality segmentation and localization labels are not yet available. Performance increases with larger training sets, suggesting further data expansion could improve models.
rai:dataUseCases: Training, validation, and testing of AI models for: (1) multi-abnormality detection in 3D chest CT volumes (zero-shot and supervised), (2) CT volume retrieval (volume-to-volume and report-to-volume), (3) radiology report generation, (4) visual question answering for 3D chest CT, (5) contrastive language-image pretraining for 3D medical imaging, (6) fine-tuning vision-language models for clinical applications. The dataset supports both self-supervised and supervised learning approaches. Not recommended for clinical deployment without further validation.
